title: Response Formatting
description: Learn how to structure API responses so clients always know what to expect, with consistent envelopes, proper status codes, and clear error shapes.

data.text: A well-formatted response does more than return data. It tells the client whether the request succeeded, what the data means, and what to do next. Consistency across endpoints makes frontend code simpler and debugging faster.
A common pattern is to wrap successful responses in a predictable envelope. Instead of returning raw data, include metadata like pagination info, request IDs, or timestamps that clients often need.

data.title: Consistent success response envelope

data.text: Status codes communicate the result of the request without the client having to inspect the body. Use the right code for the situation so HTTP clients, proxies, and browsers can react appropriately.

rows: Successful POST that creates a resource
Successful DELETE or update with no body to return

data.text: Errors should be just as structured as successes. A consistent error shape lets frontend code show user-friendly messages without parsing different formats for each endpoint.

data.title: Consistent error response shape
Do Not Leak Internal Details
data.text: In production, avoid returning stack traces or database error messages to clients. Log those details server-side and return a generic message to the user. Detailed errors help attackers and confuse normal users.

Always set `Content-Type: application/json` for JSON responses. If your API is called from a browser on a different origin, configure CORS headers carefully so only trusted domains can call your endpoints.

data.title: Setting CORS headers on a response
Key Takeaways
items: Use a success envelope with `success: true` and a `data` field
Pick the correct HTTP status code for every outcome
Return a structured error envelope with `success: false` and an `error` object
Set proper `Content-Type` and CORS headers for browser clients
